source_refs.note: Book p. 12: 1.4 Three Cube Roots of Unity, Note box

blocks.text: "Unity" means the number 1. A cube root of unity is a number whose cube is 1. In real numbers only 1 itself works, but in complex numbers there are three cube roots of unity. Let \(x\) be a cube root of unity. Then

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The factorization uses \(a^{3} - b^{3} = (a - b)(a^{2} + ab + b^{2})\) with \(a = x\), \(b = 1\). A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero, so we get two equations.
Either \(x - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 1\), or \(x^{2} + x + 1 = 0\). By the quadratic formula (\(a = b = c = 1\)):

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the middle step as \(\frac{1 \pm \sqrt{3}i}{2}\); the minus sign of \(-1\) is missing. Correctly: \(x = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1-4}}{2} = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{-3}}{2} = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\), as the book's next line shows.
Thus, the three cube roots of unity are:

blocks.text_alt: 1, minus 1 plus root 3 i over 2, and minus 1 minus root 3 i over 2

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: We know that the numbers containing \(i\) are called Complex numbers. So \(\frac{-1+\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\) and \(\frac{-1-\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\) are called complex or imaginary cube roots of unity.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
\(\sqrt{3}i\) in the book means \(\sqrt{3}\cdot i\) (the \(i\) is outside the root).
Quick check that \(\frac{-1+\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\) really is a cube root of 1: its square is \(\frac{1 - 2\sqrt{3}\,i - 3}{4} = \frac{-1-\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\), and multiplying the two complex roots gives \(\frac{(-1)^{2} - (\sqrt{3}\,i)^{2}}{4} = \frac{1 + 3}{4} = 1\). So its cube is 1.
The two complex roots are conjugates of each other (only the sign of the imaginary part differs).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. The cube roots of unity are the roots of \(x^{3} = 1\): \(1\), \(\frac{-1+\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\), \(\frac{-1-\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\).
2. They come from \((x - 1)(x^{2} + x + 1) = 0\).
3. One root is real (1); the other two are complex conjugates.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Saying 1 has only one cube root: in \(C\) it has three.
2. Losing the minus sign of \(-b\) in the quadratic formula (the book itself does this in one line): with \(b = 1\), \(-b = -1\).
3. Writing \(\sqrt{-3} = -\sqrt{3}\): it is \(\sqrt{3}\,i\).
